system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2198-02-08 11:34:00 to 2198-02-12 15:30:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 30-year-old woman with Type 1 diabetes and a history of gastroparesis s/p gastric pacer presented with acute nausea and vomiting, one week after a prior hospitalization for similar symptoms. She had recently received a Botox injection for gastroparesis and reported coffee-ground emesis. She was admitted for inability to tolerate oral intake and managed with IV fluids, antiemetics (ondansetron, metoclopramide, compazine), and proton pump inhibition. Her hypertension, exacerbated by vomiting and anxiety, was controlled with IV metoprolol and transitioned to oral lisinopril. Abdominal imaging showed no obstruction or ileus. She gradually improved, tolerating a soft diet and oral medications. Her sodium was noted to be low (130) on discharge but asymptomatic; outpatient labs were ordered. She was discharged home in stable condition with new prescriptions for metoclopramide, pantoprazole, ondansetron, and lisinopril, and follow-up planned with gastroenterology for pacer evaluation.
problems: Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type I [juvenile type], not stated as uncontrolled

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this hospital stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I woke up this morning at 6 with really bad nausea and started vomiting. It’s been happening all day. I just got out of the hospital a few days ago for the same thing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And how have you been feeling since your last discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was doing okay. I was eating a little, taking my Reglan, Protonix, Zofran, and lisinopril like I was told. I thought I was past this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The vomiting—has it been bloody or dark like coffee grounds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s been greenish—bilious, I think. No blood. I did pass gas and had a bowel movement this morning, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. Any fevers, chest pain, or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing like that. Just the nausea and vomiting. I feel weak and kind of foggy from the Ativan they gave me in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Your blood pressure was high when you came in—168 over 87—and your heart rate was fast. We’ll keep an eye on that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it usually goes up when I’m stressed or vomiting a lot. Is that still a concern?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re managing it. You got IV metoprolol in the ER, and we’ll restart your lisinopril once you can keep things down. For now, we’re keeping you NPO—nothing by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I understand. What about my insulin? I’m worried about my sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We’re giving you IV fluids with some insulin to manage your blood sugar. Your glucose was 274 when you arrived. We’ll switch back to your usual insulin regimen as you start eating again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been trying so hard to stay on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. I wanted to update you on your labs. Your white count was high this morning—13.2—but it’s already coming down. We checked blood cultures to rule out infection, and they came back negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no infection? That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s good. Your chest X-ray was clear too—no pneumonia or other issues. We think this is another flare of your gastroparesis, especially since it feels just like your last episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’ve been taking my meds. Why is this happening again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes even with good medication adherence, gastroparesis can flare. Your gastric pacer was adjusted just a week ago—could be part of the reason your stomach is still unstable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. I forgot about that. So what now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep giving you IV fluids and anti-nausea meds—Zofran, Compazine, and Ativan as needed. We’re also continuing your Protonix and Reglan through IV for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are improving. Your white count is down to 6.6, and your sodium is a bit low—130—but stable. We’re watching it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is low sodium serious? I had that last time too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but yours isn’t causing symptoms. It’s likely due to vomiting and fluid shifts. We’re not giving extra sodium, but we’ll monitor it. Your TSH and cortisol were normal, so it’s not a hormone issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. Can I try sipping water yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re going to start with 5 mL sips of clear liquids every 15 minutes. If you keep that down for a few hours, we’ll advance to toast and tea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’m so ready to eat something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. Just checking in. The nurse said you’ve kept down small sips and had a bit of toast. How’s your nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Still a little queasy, but not vomiting. I even took my Reglan pill without throwing it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent progress. We’ll keep advancing your diet slowly—BRAT diet for now: bananas, rice, applesauce, toast. Low fat, low fiber.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my insulin? I took my long-acting at bedtime, but I’m not eating my usual meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping your glargine at bedtime. For your lispro, we’re using a sliding scale based on your blood sugar since you’re not on regular meals yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture came back. It showed mixed bacteria, but that’s likely contamination from skin or genital flora—nothing to treat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no UTI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, no infection. Your electrolytes are stable, and your abdomen is soft and not tender. This is looking like pure gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it’s not something new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. You’ve been tolerating oral meds and a soft diet for over 24 hours. We’re thinking you could go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the BRAT diet and advance slowly. Keep taking your Reglan with meals, Protonix twice daily, and your insulin as directed. We’re adding a new medication—prochlorperazine—for breakthrough nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that like Compazine? I’ve used that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, same medication. You can take one tablet every six hours as needed. Also, keep using Zofran if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure and sodium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your BP is stable on lisinopril. For sodium, it’s still a bit low—131—but you’re not having symptoms. Follow up with your PCP in a few weeks to check it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should I worry if I start vomiting again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you can’t keep fluids down for more than 12 hours, or if you feel weak or dizzy, come back. Otherwise, keep using your anti-nausea meds and stay in touch with your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have an appointment with Dr. ___ this week to check the gastric pacer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Also, your heart murmur and mild LVH—we don’t think it’s related to this admission, but please follow up with your PCP about cardiology if you haven’t already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. You’re doing well—eating, keeping meds down, and walking around. Here’s your prescription list and instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I’m really glad to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it slow, follow the diet, and don’t hesitate to call your doctors if you have concerns. We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge papers and prescriptions shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—keep monitoring your blood sugar closely, especially as you start eating more normally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve been doing fingersticks every four hours like always.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Once you’re back on your regular diet, resume your usual insulin sliding scale.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll write that down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care and feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 30-year-old woman with Type 1 diabetes and a history of gastroparesis s/p gastric pacer presented with recurrent nausea and vomiting, just days after a prior discharge for similar symptoms. She had been tolerating oral intake until the morning of admission when she developed bilious, nonbloody vomiting. She was managed with NPO status, IV fluids, and IV antiemetics including ondansetron, prochlorperazine, and ativan. Her blood pressure, elevated on presentation, was controlled with IV metoprolol and transitioned back to oral lisinopril. Laboratory evaluation showed transient leukocytosis that resolved, mild hyponatremia (Na 130-132) likely due to vomiting and inappropriate ADH, and stable renal function. Blood and urine cultures showed no true infection. She gradually improved over 36 hours, advancing to a BRAT diet and oral medications. By discharge, she was tolerating oral intake, ambulating independently, and had stable vital signs. She was discharged home with continued antiemetics, insulin management guidance, and follow-up appointments with gastroenterology for pacer evaluation and her PCP for hypertension, hyponatremia, and cardiology referral.
